summary: Draft Control Power record. `AllowAudioToEnableExecutionRequiredPowerRequests` sits under `HKLM\\SYSTEM\\CurrentControlSet\\Control\\Power`, has an explicit repo-doc default of `1`, is absent on the observed clean baseline, produced an exact current-build Unicode string hit in `ntoskrnl.exe`, and was later retained by source-enrichment as a docs-first kernel candidate with a `power-request-simulation` trigger recommendation. A later repo-native follow-up then exposed that same trigger family as a named guest Procmon profile and mega-trigger runtime alias. Later KVM local-KD passes first surfaced the exact symbol `nt!PopPowerRequestActiveAudioEnablesExecutionRequired` and then resolved its live current-build value as `1`, aligning the running kernel with the repo-doc default. A later current-build disassembly pass then showed a direct consumer in `nt!PopPowerRequestEvaluateExecutionRequiredStatus`. Later follow-ups then showed `nt!PopUmpoSendPowerRequestOverrideQuery` packaging requester state for `nt!PopUmpoSendPowerMessage`, `nt!PopPowerRequestExecutionRequiredSettingCallback` staying timeout-setting specific by updating `nt!PopExecutionRequiredTimeout`, and the timeout timer/worker chain feeding back into `nt!PopPowerRequestHandleExecutionEnablementUpdate`. The lane is strong enough for a schema-backed draft, but still lacks a registry seeding path and an exact runtime registry read.

setting.name: Allow Audio To Enable Execution Required Power Requests
setting.casual_explanation: This appears to be a kernel-adjacent Control Power setting tied to whether active audio can enable execution-required power requests. It is being tracked as a research candidate, not a user-facing tweak.
setting.why_people_change_it: Kernel and power researchers may inspect this value when investigating how active audio sessions influence execution-required power-request behavior under undocumented power-policy flows.
setting.tradeoffs_overview: The value now has a stronger evidence chain because it has repo docs, observed baseline state, an exact current-build string hit, a retained enrichment recommendation, a repo-native trigger harness, a live KVM local-KD value that matches the repo-doc default, direct current-build consumer disassembly, a visible UMPO override-query lineage, a timeout-setting callback disassembly, and a retained timeout timer/worker chain. It is still too weak for a published tweak because no current-build registry seeding path has been demonstrated and an exact runtime registry read remains unresolved.
setting.professional_notes: Repo power docs assign `AllowAudioToEnableExecutionRequiredPowerRequests = 1` under `Control\\Power` and map it to `PopPowerRequestActiveAudioEnablesExecutionRequired`. The power routing note later kept the value inside the `Control\\Power` docs cluster. The observed clean baseline then confirmed that the parent `Control\\Power` path exists while the value itself is absent. A later targeted current-build string batch found an exact Unicode hit for `AllowAudioToEnableExecutionRequiredPowerRequests` in `ntoskrnl.exe`, which is stronger than a pure docs-only mention and enough to keep the value out of raw backlog. Source-enrichment later retained the candidate in the canonical queue with `power-request-simulation` as the suggested trigger family, specifically `PowerCreateRequest(SystemRequired)`, `PowerSetRequest(DisplayRequired)`, and an audio playback session. A later repo-native follow-up then exposed that same trigger family as a named guest Procmon profile plus a matching mega-trigger runtime alias, closing the old trigger-design gap before the first dedicated narrow replay. Later KVM local-KD passes first surfaced the exact symbol `nt!PopPowerRequestActiveAudioEnablesExecutionRequired` and then read its live current-build value as `1`, which matches the repo-doc default and keeps the lane out of pure docs-first territory. A later current-build disassembly pass then showed `nt!PopPowerRequestEvaluateExecutionRequiredStatus` directly comparing `nt!PopPowerRequestActiveAudioEnablesExecutionRequired` against the caller-supplied execution-required state, while `nt!PopPowerRequestExecutionRequiredSettingCallback` chained into the same reader family through `PopPowerRequestHandleExecutionmentUpdate`. A later wildcard lineage pass then showed that the current build exposes only one `*PowerRequest*Setting*` symbol, `nt!PopPowerRequestExecutionRequiredSettingCallback`, alongside `PopPowerRequestInitialize`, `PopPowerRequestOverrideInitialize`, and the `PopExecutionRequiredTimeout` family. A later init/override disassembly pass then showed `PopPowerRequestInitialize` only zeroing per-object fields and `PopPowerRequestOverrideInitialize` iterating `PopPowerRequestObjectList` before calling `PopUmpoSendPowerRequestOverrideQuery`, which is useful because it still did not expose a registry read in the visible current-build init path. A later dedicated UMPO disassembly pass then showed `PopUmpoSendPowerRequestOverrideQuery` storing requester identity via `PoStoreRequester`, allocating an `Umpo`-tagged buffer, and dispatching `PopUmpoSendPowerMessage`, while wildcard output exposed `PopUmpoSendPowerRequestCreate`, `PopUmpoSendPowerRequestAction`, and `PopUmpoSendPowerRequestOverrideCleanup`. A later dedicated callback disassembly pass then showed `PopPowerRequestExecutionRequiredSettingCallback` comparing the incoming GUID against `GUID_EXECUTION_REQUIRED_REQUEST_TIMEOUT`, requiring a 4-byte payload, writing `PopExecutionRequiredTimeout`, rearming `PopPowerRequestExecutionRequiredTimeoutTimer`, and then calling `PopPowerRequestHandleExecutionEnablementUpdate`. A later timeout-lineage pass then showed `PopPowerRequestSetExecutionRequiredTimeoutTimer` reading `PopExecutionRequiredTimeout`, comparing it against `PopExecutionRequiredContext`, and arming `PopPowerRequestExecutionRequiredTimeoutTimer` via `KeSetTimer2`, while `PopPowerRequestExecutionRequiredTimeoutCallback` simply queued work and `PopPowerRequestExecutionRequiredTimeoutWorker` re-entered `PopPowerRequestHandleExecutionEnablementUpdate`. This matters because the visible family is now callback/init/timeout-setting/timer-worker/UMPO driven and still does not demonstrate a registry read or a direct write to `PopPowerRequestActiveAudioEnablesExecutionRequired`. The next proof step is no longer a generic reader hunt; it is whether any registry seeding path exists outside this visible family on modern builds.
